comments.body:
DESIGN BRAINSTORM — open→in_progress "plan-review" verification gate (mirror of the completion-verifier close gate). Status: design largely converged; tuning + write-up of design-of-record pending DSO data mining.

GOAL: a verification workflow that runs when a ticket is claimed (open→in_progress), reviewing the ticket's implementation plan BEFORE an agent executes it — the inverse of the completion-verifier (which runs at close). It is a rebar FEATURE used by DIVERSE CLIENT PROJECTS (many languages/frameworks/structures); design judged by cross-language generalization, NOT rebar's own codebase. (Correction logged: rebar is Python with legacy bash being strangled; an earlier "rebar is heavily bash" claim was a conflation with DSO and was deleted.)

CONVERGED DESIGN (two-layer):
- Trigger/enforcement: fires at open→in_progress. `claim` = FAST check for a valid signed plan-review attestation; the heavy review runs OUT-OF-BAND. It is a REVIEW PROCESS, not a dialog — the CLIENT revises the plan and RE-RUNS the review to earn a fresh signature (mirrors completion-verifier: returns FAIL+findings, blocks close, client fixes+recloses). rebar owns the review/verdict/findings/signature/invalidation; it does NOT own a revise loop.
- Routing pivots on has_children (not ticket type).
- Attestation binding (scope (i)): signature bound to the latest MATERIAL event commit on the tickets branch — edits to description / acceptance-criteria / file_impact / decomposition INVALIDATE (force re-review); tags / comments / links / assignee do NOT (no re-review treadmill). Justification: the cert asserts "process followed against THIS plan"; honoring it after a material edit would falsely certify content never reviewed.
- Certificate semantics (Joe's framing): "we ran our process to the best of our ability given this codebase, and no red flags were raised" — NOT "this plan is perfect." Fail-open is DESIRED. Record COVERAGE (which sound checks ran vs skipped-unsupported) for transparency.
- LAYER 1 — deterministic + structural gate (the ONLY thing that blocks; convergent by construction): frozen binary MET/UNMET rubric. Checks: P1 readiness shape (standardized `## Acceptance Criteria` ALL types), P2 file/symbol/import resolution (LSP/tree-sitter, NOT llm-grep), P3 package/dep existence (manifest/lockfile+registry), P4 oversize signals (config-tunable), P5 task-DAG validity + cross-task interference, P6 AC/DD quality (compound-AND, vague-lexicon, spec-fidelity, verify-command robustness — POLYGLOT FIX: shell-specific verify-cmd sub-checks fail-open/advisory when not POSIX shell), P7 destructive/irreversible sniff (escalation signal only).
- LAYER 2 — advisory LLM review (NEVER blocks; surfaces findings): the judgment criteria (F1 measurability & agent-in-session-completability, F4 user/problem present, E1 coherence + terminology-consistency + duplicate-requirements, E2 ambiguity + spike/research-undercooked + explicit-decision-deferral, E3 intent fidelity [2-step blind-restate→compare, child-vs-slice], E5 testing-plan completeness, E6 verification/termination + end-state-reachability, G1+G2 edit-set/scope accuracy [target-first then deterministic consumer lookup; high-blast≠fail], G3 child coverage [4-bucket+3-condition], G4 child consistency [7 categories], E4 assumption/premise verification [forced codebase probe, ban cached-context], A1 anti-slop/NIH/config-proliferation/Rule-of-Three) PLUS one BOUNDED broad open-ended pass for unknown-unknowns. Triggered overlays (router-LLM selects relevance): T1 prior-art/novel-arch, T2 empirical probe, T3 integration feasibility, T4 compat/destructiveness-as-explicit-choice, T5a-e perf/reliability/security/a11y/maintainability, T6 UX, T7 docs (+invalidated+hot-path bloat), T8 LLM-prompt antipatterns, T9 shared-state lifecycle (CREATE/UPDATE/CONSUME/RETIRE).

KEY REBALANCE (load-bearing, from Opus critical review + Joe): plan review's dominant failure is FALSE-NEGATIVE / rubber-stamp (Kambhampati: LLM judges accept 84% of invalid plans), NOT code-review's false-positive. The elaborate anti-FP contract I'd built was a CODE-REVIEW import (rebar's code-reviewer agents, DSO reviewer-base) and was wrong for plan review. So: RECALL-FIRST — sound/deterministic checks BLOCK; LLM judgment ADVISES/SURFACES; anti-FP stripped to minimal (single benign-reading filter + anti-fabrication instruction). Dropped: cite-or-omit-as-universal-gate (fails for omissions — ground the REQUIREMENT instead, never ask open-ended "what's missing": AbsenceBench) and reachable-harm bar (no impl at plan time — use blockingness-to-criteria severity). Dropped severity-minor-floor (code-review concept, defer to tuning). Dropped per-dimension calibrated abstention (needs a gold set we likely can't get → surface-on-uncertainty instead).

VERDICT MODEL: per-criterion PASS / AMBIGUOUS / FAIL. AMBIGUOUS = non-blocking → escalate to higher-tier adjudicator. FAIL→block per-dimension: sound checks block immediately (near-zero FP); judgment dims advisory (the field keeps LLM plan-review advisory, not blocking, BECAUSE of the rubber-stamp problem). Binary checklists WHERE criteria decompose cleanly (most DET + structural); graded/narrative where genuinely qualitative (intent fidelity, decomposition, the broad pass).

CONFIGURABLE CHUNKING (Joe's reconciliation of cost-vs-quality + local-vs-frontier clients): the partition of criteria across LLM calls is a PROJECT KNOB — fewer/larger calls (frontier models: cost-effective, comparable quality) ↔ more/smaller per-criterion calls (local/small models: less context-limit risk, more reliable). Default "in the middle" (grouped chunks). Replaces the "single structured pass" crystallization. The criteria registry maps to chunks per config.

LAYER-2 LOOP RESOLUTION (Joe caught a muddle): there is NO internal refine loop and NO second broad pass within a single review — the reviewer runs once per invocation and returns findings. The only "loop" is the CLIENT re-invoking after revising. Convergence is FREE because Layer 1 (deterministic, frozen binary rubric) is the SOLE blocker — all-MET is a guaranteed fixed point regardless of advisory findings. On re-invocation, review the CURRENT plan FRESH (don't limit to prior findings when the plan changed). diff-only re-review = OPTIONAL cost-saver, NOT a convergence mechanism. Caveat: the reviewer must NOT be the same model/instance that authored the plan (self-preference bias; generator≠critic).

PROPORTIONATE SCRUTINY + ESCALATION: review depth scales with complexity (small task = DET + one cheap pass; epic/has_children = full depth). Escalation-to-stronger-model factors = SIZE + COMPLEXITY + CENTRALITY (DSO has hooks/lib/centrality.sh + blast-radius-score.py). Risk posture is PROJECT-CONFIGURABLE with a sensible default (to be anchored to DSO ticket data). Budget caps: criterion/chunk-ATOMIC checkpointing (no half-criterion waste; order by priority so a cap sheds lowest-value criteria); Layer 1 always completes (cheap); on Layer-2 budget hit → a NON-TERMINAL "incomplete/inconclusive" outcome — NOT failed (cap is external to the ticket), NOT certified (process didn't complete) — client raises budget / re-runs / escalates.

TOOLING (polyglot, fail-open IRONCLAD): solidlsp (Serena's LSP lib — ALREADY in this repo) + ast-grep (P2 resolution, G1 callers); syft + per-ecosystem registry HTTP + LLM-fallback (P3 deps); scc + lizard (P4 size/CCN); ast-grep/tree-sitter (G2 locus). Unsupported lang / no server / crash / timeout → skipped = PASS, NEVER fail; hard "missing" only from top-tier servers (pyright/gopls/rust-analyzer/tsserver/clangd). This is the only reason the deterministic tier generalizes across clients. Avoid stack-graphs (archived), Glean (over-engineered); osv-scanner ≠ existence oracle.

EXTENSIBILITY: a dimension is a declarative REGISTRY DESCRIPTOR; the orchestrator is generic (never names a dimension). Reuse rebar's existing rebar.llm extension points (reviewer catalog.json + contracts.py + prompt files + pluggable runner). Criteria registry = frozen WITHIN a review loop (convergence), extended BETWEEN versions (growth). Implement ALL criteria in ONE WAVE (no v1/deferred), decomposed into appropriately-sized tasks with dependencies; dogfood by tracking the decomposition in rebar.

BUGS: PARKED — ship with bug-type tickets SKIPPED + a follow-on epic (their format/content differs markedly from planning tickets; bugs often lack a plan at claim because you investigate first). Revisit after the tuning question. Interim principle: has_plan-driven — a planless ticket is N/A, not FAIL.

OUT OF SCOPE (confirmed): cross-ticket no-overlap / dependency-aware (deterministic file-impact/link now; semantic backlog-scan → follow-on); propose-multiple-then-select loop (authoring, not review); cross-service deploy topology (not in-session-verifiable); DSO's dogfooding/staged-rollout/7-day-monitor validation (violates agent-completable-in-session); all-equal-5 / scalar-trait gating; project-supplied dimensions (FUTURE seam, design-for not built); E8 test-gaming (post-impl, → code-review/close gate).

RESEARCH DONE (~16 subagents): full from-scratch DSO re-exploration (8 chunked agents → lossless dimension catalog; coverage-ledger methodology after an initial single-agent pass missed surfaces); two GitHub/OSS prior-art passes (general LLM-plan-review; LLM-implements-the-plan); LLM-planning failure-modes; scoping + plan-appropriate anti-FP; scoped-vs-broad + convergence; Opus critical review. Key external anchors: AbsenceBench 2506.11440 (LLMs bad at detecting omissions), Kambhampati 2310.08118 (84% false-accept), MAST 2503.13657 (~44% of agent failures are spec/plan defects), Agent GPA 2510.08847 (coherence as a dimension), CheckEval/TICKing 2410.03608 (binary checklists raise agreement), convergence (cap + severity-gating + diff-only; field keeps LLM plan-review ADVISORY not blocking due to rubber-stamp + non-determinism). Field reality: most ship a single HOLISTIC pass (cost) + HUMAN approval gate (rubber-stamp problem); per-dimension + blocking-LLM-gate is rare — our per-dimension registry is a deliberate, evidenced bet.

ARTIFACTS (job-local /tmp, ephemeral — substance captured here): dso-dimension-catalog-v2.md (lossless DSO dimension union), our-review-dimensions-v2.md / v3.md (design evolution). v4 design-of-record NOT yet written.

OPEN / NEXT: DSO ticket-data mining agent RUNNING — characterize the DSO ticket corpus (sizes/types/complexity/outcomes), extract a stratified example library, propose concrete complexity→depth thresholds + escalation factors (size/complexity/centrality) + chunking default, and assess the corpus as a gold-ish tuning/eval set for over/under-review risk. AFTER it lands → write the v4 design-of-record (Layer-1/Layer-2 + configurable chunking + budget-incomplete status + escalation), then decompose into the rebar implementation epic (one wave, tasks with deps). PENDING JOE: approve the proportionate-depth posture / thresholds, the budget posture, and confirm the bug-skip + follow-on-epic.

=== RESEARCH REPORT ===
=== prior-art: agile DoR / INVEST / story-splitting / LLM-as-judge / RFC prior-art
=== agent a92b1fca9a73a16b8

All verification checks pass cleanly. Every load-bearing claim I spot-checked — across all six research areas — was confirmed verbatim against primary sources. One refinement: the Humanizing Work guide has two authors (Richard Lawrence and Peter Green), not Lawrence alone. With verification complete, here is the synthesized report.

---

# Research Report: Prior Art for an Automated Ticket-Readiness / Plan-Verification Gate

Scope: published practice and research relevant to an LLM-driven gate that runs when a work ticket moves open → in-progress, to catch oversized/ambiguous work, inaccurate file references, plans that ignore consumers or tests, unvalidated novel architecture, AC/description mismatch, and incomplete child coverage. All key claims (arXiv IDs, attributions, thresholds, template wording) were adversarially verified against primary sources; verification notes are flagged inline.

---

## 1. Definition of Ready (DoR)

**Key concept.** DoR is a team's explicit, shared set of entry criteria a backlog item must meet *before* it is pulled into a sprint and started — the entry-gate analog of the Definition of Done's exit gate. Crucially, **DoR is not in the Scrum Guide** (DoD is a formal Scrum commitment; DoR is an optional complementary practice), and it is conventionally tied to the INVEST heuristic.

**DoR vs DoD (the clean framing):** "The Definition of Ready covers the requirements *coming into* the sprint; the Definition of Done covers the product *coming out of* the sprint." DoR applies to individual backlog items; DoD applies to the Increment.

**Reusable DoR checklist** (consolidated from Atlassian, Scrum Alliance, Agile Alliance, Mountain Goat). A story is Ready when: user story is clear/well-formed; business value is articulated; **acceptance criteria are defined, measurable, and testable**; the team shares understanding of it; it is small enough to fit one sprint; it is estimated; dependencies are identified and resolved; there are no blockers; UX/design is attached where applicable; INVEST is satisfied; stakeholders are aligned.

**Important controversy (directly relevant to a *gate*).** DoR is widely criticized as an anti-pattern *when it hardens into a mandatory approval gate*. Mike Cohn warns a strict DoR becomes "a huge step towards a sequential, stage-gate approach"; Scrum Alliance says it can "place documentation, processes, and sticking to a plan over individuals, interactions, and collaboration — the inverse of the Agile Manifesto." The recurring recommendation: keep DoR as a **flexible guideline / conversation prompt**, not a hard pass/fail bar. For your design, this argues for a gate that *advises and surfaces* problems (and is overridable) rather than one that hard-blocks — mirroring rebar's existing `--force-close` escape hatch.

**Sources:**
- Mike Cohn / Mountain Goat — "The Definition of Ready and Its Dangers" — https://www.mountaingoatsoftware.com/blog/the-dangers-of-a-definition-of-ready
- Agile Alliance glossary — "Definition of Ready" — https://agilealliance.org/glossary/definition-of-ready/ (defines DoR as criteria "generally based on the INVEST matrix")
- Scrum Alliance — "Pros and Cons of a Definition of Ready" — https://resources.scrumalliance.org/Article/pros-cons-definition-ready
- Scrum.org — "Difference Between the DoD and the DoR" — https://www.scrum.org/resources/blog/what-difference-between-definition-done-dod-and-definition-ready-dor
- Atlassian — "Definition of Ready" — https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/definition-of-ready

---

## 2. INVEST (and analogs for tasks/bugs/epics)

**Origin (verified).** Bill Wake, "INVEST in Good Stories, and SMART Tasks," XP123, **August 17, 2003** — https://xp123.com/invest-in-good-stories-and-smart-tasks/. Popularized by Mike Cohn's *User Stories Applied* (2004).

**The six (verified verbatim):** **I**ndependent, **N**egotiable, **V**aluable (Agile Alliance phrases it "Valuable *or vertical*" — a vertical slice), **E**stimable, **S**mall ("so as to fit within an iteration"), **T**estable ("in principle, even if there isn't a test yet").

**Operationalizing "Small" / too-big (automatable signals):**
- Story-point ceiling: a common rule is split anything **> 8 points** before sprint planning; Atlassian cites **~16 hours / ~20 points** as "too hard to estimate confidently → break down."
- The **6–10-stories-per-sprint** rule of thumb (Humanizing Work): if you can't fit 6–10 into a sprint, stories are too big.
- Can't fit in one sprint = the canonical too-big signal; that is also the definition of an epic.
- Structural/linguistic: conjunctions ("and"/"or"), the verb **"manage"** (and other CRUD-umbrella verbs), many AC items spanning different concerns, multiple personas, multiple workflow steps.

**Analogs for other types:**
- **Tasks → SMART** (Wake's own analog, same 2003 article, verified): **S**pecific, **M**easurable, **A**chievable, **R**elevant, **T**ime-boxed.
- **Bugs → "ready" field set** (industry consensus, no single acronym): title, **steps to reproduce**, **expected vs actual**, environment, severity/impact, visual evidence. This maps directly onto rebar's bug template (`## Reproduction Steps` + Expected vs Actual).
- **Epics → well-formed criteria:** clear narrative, high-level AC + scope boundary, a **measurable success metric** (outcome-focused, not technical spec), too big for one sprint by definition, decomposes into ~3–10 stories. Maps onto rebar's `## Success Criteria` / `## Context`.

**Critiques worth knowing.** Wake himself called **Estimable** "the most-abused aspect of INVEST (most energy for least value)" and later suggested swapping E=Estimable → **E=External**. **Independent** is an ideal, not a gate. Meta-critique: INVEST gets weaponized as a "bouncer" that blocks work — again arguing against a rigid gate.

**Sources:**
- Bill Wake — https://xp123.com/invest-in-good-stories-and-smart-tasks/
- Agile Alliance — "INVEST" — https://agilealliance.org/glossary/invest/
- Maarten Dalmijn — "Revisiting INVEST 20+ Years Later" — https://mdalmijn.com/p/revisiting-invest-20-years-later
- Atlassian — "Epics, Stories, Themes" — https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/epics-stories-themes

---

## 3. Story splitting / decomposition

**SPIDR (Mike Cohn) — verified.** "Almost every story can be split with one of five techniques": **S**pike (time-boxed research for unknowns; last resort), **P**ath (multiple ways to accomplish the goal), **I**nterface (split by platform/device, or simple-UI-first), **D**ata (subset of data first), **R**ules (temporarily relax business rules). — https://www.mountaingoatsoftware.com/blog/five-simple-but-powerful-ways-to-split-user-stories

**Richard Lawrence & Peter Green — "How to Split a User Story" (Humanizing Work) — verified.** A 3-step flowchart (confirm it's a valuable story meeting INVEST except "Small" → apply a pattern → evaluate splits, preferring those that reveal deprioritizable work and yield comparable sizes) plus **9 patterns**: Workflow Steps, Business Rule Variations, Major Effort, Simple/Complex, Variations in Data, Data Entry Methods, Deferred Performance, **Operations (CRUD)** — where "the word 'manage' is a giveaway that the story covers multiple operations" — and Break Out a Spike. Includes the verified **6–10 stories per sprint** size rule. (Note: authored by Lawrence *and* Green, not Lawrence alone.) — https://www.humanizingwork.com/the-humanizing-work-guide-to-splitting-user-stories/ · Flowchart PDF: https://www.humanizingwork.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/HW-Story-Splitting-Flowchart.pdf

**Vertical vs horizontal slicing.** Vertical = thin end-to-end cut delivering user-visible value (recommended; preserves INVEST "Valuable"). Horizontal = split by technical layer (anti-pattern; no slice delivers value alone). Core principle: every slice must independently deliver end-to-end value.

**Directly automatable "too big" signals (the most reusable part for your gate):**

| Signal | Detection | Strength |
|---|---|---|
| Conjunctions "and/or/but/with" in title/narrative | regex / token scan — "first thing to do with a big story" | Strong |
| Too many acceptance criteria | count `- [ ]` items vs threshold (cited ranges: ideally 1–3 / "<5"; ">12 too large") | Strong |
| CRUD / "manage" / "configure" verbs | keyword set {manage, configure, administer, create, read, update, delete, search} | Strong (Lawrence) |
| Multiple personas | count `As a <role>` clauses; >1 → candidate | Medium |
| Multiple workflow steps | sequence words (then/after/first…next) | Medium |
| Multiple data types/channels | lists of variants (web/mobile/API, iOS/Android) | Medium |
| Estimate ≥ threshold | story points ≥ cap (Atlassian: ~20 pts) | Strong (needs metadata) |

**Sources:** Cohn SPIDR (above); Humanizing Work (above); Atlassian — "Decomposing user stories in Jira" — https://www.atlassian.com/blog/development/break-decomposing-user-stories-jira (too-big signals: "sounds like a feature," can't fit a sprint, "20 story points or more").

---

## 4. LLM-as-judge & agent-planning verification

**Seminal LLM-as-judge — verified.** Zheng et al., "Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena," **arXiv:2306.05685** (NeurIPS 2023). GPT-4 judges **match human preferences at >80% agreement** (≈ human-human agreement). Three named biases (the canonical taxonomy): **position**, **verbosity**, **self-enhancement** (plus weak math/logic grading). Three reusable judging modes: **pairwise comparison**, **single-answer grading**, **reference-guided grading**. — https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685

**Grading issues/PRs/specs with LLMs:**
- **microsoft/LLM-RUBRIC** (ACL 2024) — multidimensional, *calibrated* rubric; the LLM is asked **one rubric question at a time** and outputs a distribution, then a calibration net maps to human ratings. The most directly reusable "rubric judge" reference. — https://github.com/microsoft/LLM-Rubric
- **Sphinx** — checklist-based benchmark for LLM-driven PR review, scoring coverage of structured verification points — https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.04252
- **GitHub blog** — review agent PRs by **separating the analysis step from execution with an approval gate** (directly your open→in-progress gate pattern) — https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/generative-ai/agent-pull-requests-are-everywhere-heres-how-to-review-them/
- **Anthropic — "Demystifying evals for AI agents"** — pair deterministic checks (test suites) with model-based rubric graders — https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents

**Plan critics / self-critique loops (papers):**
- **Reflexion** (Shinn et al.) — verbal self-reflection in an episodic memory buffer; **91% pass@1 on HumanEval vs GPT-4's 80%** (verified) — arXiv:2303.11366
- **Self-Refine** (Madaan et al.) — generate → self-feedback → refine — arXiv:2303.17651
- **CRITIC** (Gou et al., ICLR 2024) — tool-grounded critique; key caution: **LLMs cannot reliably self-correct *without external grounding*** — arXiv:2305.11738
- **Chain-of-Verification (CoVe)** — draft → plan verification questions → **answer them independently** → finalize; highly reusable for plan-checking — arXiv:2309.11495
- **LLM-Modulo** — LLM-generator + sound external verifier in a generate-test loop; **~4.6× plan-validity gain** on TravelPlanning where CoT/ReAct/Reflexion scored ~0% — strongest evidence a *separate verifier pass* dramatically improves plan quality — arXiv:2405.20625

**Reusable rubric/critic design (synthesized from Hamel Husain, Eugene Yan, Evidently, LLM-RUBRIC):**
- Prefer **binary pass/fail** over 1–5 scores (avoids criteria drift; forces an actionable decision). If nuance needed, max 3 levels.
- Emit a structured contract per dimension: `{ dimension, reasoning (CoT first), citation (to the specific text/criterion), verdict }`. CoT-before-verdict measurably improves accuracy. This mirrors rebar's existing completion-verifier contract (FAIL must cite the failing criterion + a source citation).
- **One dimension per evaluator call** (LLM-RUBRIC). For ticket/plan grading, reusable dimensions: AC present & testable; scope clarity; actionability (files/paths/steps named); verifiability (verify commands/tests); dependencies/risks identified; no internal contradiction. Aggregate **fail-closed** (overall PASS only if all critical dimensions pass).
- **Ground the critic** (CRITIC/CoVe): have it generate verification questions and answer them against the actual codebase/artifact rather than trusting unaided self-assessment.
- **Bias controls** (Zheng): swap order for pairwise; grade substance not length (verbosity); don't use the plan's own author model as sole judge (self-enhancement).
- **Validate** the judge against hand-labels with precision/recall or Cohen's κ — *not* raw agreement (Hamel Husain https://hamel.dev/blog/posts/llm-judge/, Eugene Yan https://eugeneyan.com/writing/llm-evaluators/).

---

## 5. Prior-art research as a planning step (RFC / design-doc practice)

**Rust RFC template — verified verbatim.** Section order: Summary → Motivation → Guide-level → Reference-level → Drawbacks → **Rationale and alternatives** → **Prior art** → Unresolved questions → Future possibilities. — https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/0000-template.md

- **"Prior art"** prompting questions (verbatim): "Does this feature exist in other programming languages and what experience have their community had?" · "Is this done by some other community and what were their experiences with it?" · "What lessons can we learn from what other communities have done here?" · "Are there any published papers or great posts that discuss this?" (The template explicitly notes absence of prior art is acceptable, and precedent alone doesn't justify an RFC.)
- **"Rationale and alternatives"** (verbatim): "Why is this design the best in the space of possible designs?" · "What other designs have been considered and what is the rationale for not choosing them?" · "What is the impact of not doing this?" · "Could this be done in a library or macro instead?"

**When the heavyweight review is warranted vs skipped (Rust threshold, verbatim).** Required for "**substantial**" changes (semantic/syntactic language changes, removing features, large `std` additions). **Skipped** for: "rephrasing, reorganizing, refactoring… changing shape does not change meaning"; additions that "strictly improve objective, numerical quality criteria" (speedups, warning removal); dev-only invisible changes. — https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/README.md

**Python PEPs.** PEP 1 (normative): Rationale must "describe alternate designs that were considered"; rejected ideas "should be recorded along with the reasoning… preventing people from bringing up the same rejected idea again." PEP 12 template includes **Rationale** (mandatory) and **Rejected Ideas** (suggested). — https://peps.python.org/pep-0001/ · https://peps.python.org/pep-0012/

**Google design docs.** Malte Ubl, "Design Docs at Google" — "Alternatives considered" is "one of the most important" sections; list alternatives + the trade-offs that justify the chosen design; **skip the doc** if the solution is obvious or it'd just be "an implementation manual." — https://www.industrialempathy.com/posts/design-docs-at-google/

**ADRs / MADR.** Nygard's original ADR (Context/Decision/Consequences) — https://cognitect.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions. MADR 4.0.0 adds an explicit **"Considered Options"** list + **"Decision Outcome"** ("Chosen option … because … comes out best") + per-option "Good/Bad/Neutral, because…" — a forced trade-off comparison. — https://adr.github.io/madr/

**Synthesis for your gate:** all four ecosystems encode the same control — before adopting a novel mechanism you must (a) enumerate alternatives, (b) justify why the choice beats them on trade-offs, and (c) survey prior art — and all four **gate this behind a "substantial vs trivial" threshold** so small changes skip it. Your "plan proposes novel architecture not validated against prior art" check has direct precedent here, including the precedent for *only firing it on substantial work*.

---

## 6. Sizing / effort-estimation automation

**Story points & "too big = epic" (with thresholds).** Story points = effort + complexity + risk (Mountain Goat). Modified Fibonacci (1,2,3,5,8,13,20,40,100) — non-linear gaps deliberately force decomposition. Atlassian: estimates above **~16h / ~20 points** are "too hard to estimate confidently → break down"; an **epic = too big for one sprint, must decompose**; rule of thumb: work measured in *weeks* should be an epic. — https://www.mountaingoatsoftware.com/blog/what-are-story-points · https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/epics

**Automated estimation from issue text (papers):**
- **Deep-SE** — Choetkiertikul et al., "A deep learning model for estimating story points" — LSTM + Recurrent Highway Network on **title + description only**; benchmark of **23,313 issues / 16 projects**; beats baselines on MAE and Standardized Accuracy (all verified). arXiv:1609.00489 (IEEE TSE 2019).
- **GPT2SP** — Fu & Tantithamthavorn — fine-tuned GPT-2; 6–47% within-project MAE improvement over prior DL (IEEE TSE 49(2)).
- **LLM story-point estimation** — Shetty et al. (verified, **submitted March 2026**): **zero-shot LLMs beat supervised DL trained on 80% of the data**, on the same 16 projects. arXiv:2603.06276.

**Tools that flag oversized/stale work (published heuristics):**
- **LinearB** — PRs under **~225 LOC** (alt: ~150), **max 4 WIP stories**, alert on PRs **idle >3 days**; "almost exponential" relationship between PR size and review time; small PRs picked up ~20× faster. — https://linearb.io/blog/team-working-agreements
- **Swarmia** — issue/PR cycle time + Working-Agreement size/WIP caps with Slack alerts.
- **Jellyfish** — "stories estimated above some maximum threshold need to be broken down."

**Simplest automatable size proxies from text (ranked):**
1. **Structural footprint** (files/components mentioned, subtasks, AC count) — *most reliable*: "Early-Stage Prediction of Review Effort in AI-Generated PRs" found structural metrics hit **AUC > 0.95 vs text/CodeBERT's 0.52** (arXiv:2601.00753). For rebar this maps to **counting `set_file_impact` entries and AC checklist items**.
2. **Conjunction count** ("and"/"or") — an academic atomicity check flags noun phrases containing "and"/"or" as non-atomic/too-big (arXiv:2301.10070).
3. **Description length alone is weak/inconsistent** — use only combined with structural signals (arXiv:2507.06704).

**Sources:** Mountain Goat (above); Atlassian Fibonacci/epics (above); Deep-SE arXiv:1609.00489; Shetty et al. arXiv:2603.06276; LinearB (above); structural-footprint arXiv:2601.00753; atomicity arXiv:2301.10070.

---

## Cross-cutting takeaways for your gate design

1. **Model it as advisory, not a hard block.** The single strongest signal across DoR and INVEST literature is that readiness checklists become anti-patterns when they harden into mandatory gates. An overridable gate (like rebar's `--force-close`) that *surfaces and cites* problems aligns with both the prior art and rebar's existing "closed-without-signature is the durable signal" philosophy.
2. **Cheap structural pre-filter, then LLM.** Run automatable signals first (AC-item count, file-impact count, conjunction/verb regex, child-coverage check) and reserve the billable LLM-judge pass for tickets that pass the cheap filter or warrant deeper review — exactly the "substantial vs trivial" threshold that Rust/Google use to decide when heavyweight review fires.
3. **Borrow the verified rubric-judge contract.** One scoped binary check per dimension (LLM-RUBRIC), CoT-before-verdict, fail-closed aggregation, and every FAIL citing the failing criterion + a source citation — which is precisely the contract rebar's completion-verifier already uses, so the readiness gate can reuse that machinery.
4. **Ground the critic** (CRITIC/CoVe/LLM-Modulo): for "inaccurate file references," "ignores consumers," and "child tickets don't cover the parent," have the critic generate verification questions and check them against the actual codebase and the ticket's children — unaided self-critique is the documented failure mode.
5. **Novel-architecture check has direct RFC precedent:** force "alternatives considered + prior art surveyed," but only on substantial work — the Rust/PEP/Google/MADR "Considered Options + Rationale" sections are a ready-made rubric.

=== RESEARCH REPORT ===
=== research: agentic planning + hard-gate stress-test + generator-vs-critic
=== agent a9a9c34565b95d01b

All load-bearing claims are now verified verbatim against primary sources. The Zheng self-enhancement figures (GPT-4 +10%, Claude-v1 +25%, GPT-3.5 does not favor itself) AND the authors' own caveat are both confirmed. The Valmeekam self-critique abstract confirms the qualitative claim (the 61%/38-of-45/55-vs-88 numbers are in the body, correctly attributed). The Sinha self-conditioning and horizon claims are confirmed verbatim. The LLM-Modulo 0%/0.6%/0% figures are confirmed.

One caveat flagged by a search agent worth noting in the report: the MAST "42/37/21" category split is unverified secondary material. I have enough to synthesize. Here is the final report.

---

# Plan-verification gate for autonomous agents: a cited evidence review

**Bottom line up front:** The research strongly supports a **separate-critic, plan-time gate** for autonomous agents. The evidence converges from four independent directions: (1) the agile "gates are an anti-pattern" critique is human-specific opinion that does *not* transfer, because agents lack the in-flight adaptation that makes loose gates safe; (2) errors compound geometrically-to-worse over multi-step trajectories, so plan-time defects are the most expensive class to catch late; (3) self-critique is empirically unreliable and biased, while a *separate* critic / sound verifier produces measurable gains; (4) plan-verification-before-execution is an established, benchmarked distinct phase. The one genuinely contested design choice is **block vs. advise** — covered in the verdict.

Every quantitative claim below was verified verbatim against the primary source's abstract or HTML body.

---

## THREAD 1 — Does "hard readiness gates are an anti-pattern" transfer to autonomous agents? No.

**The human-side critique (the claim being stress-tested) is entirely practitioner opinion, and its safety mechanism is human adaptation.**

- **Mike Cohn, "The Definition of Ready and Its Dangers"** (Mountain Goat Software, 2016/upd. 2023) — https://www.mountaingoatsoftware.com/blog/the-dangers-of-a-definition-of-ready. Cohn's argument: a DoR that demands "100 percent finished before a story can be brought into an iteration" becomes "a huge step towards a sequential, stage-gate approach." His prescribed remedy is to let the team take rough/partial input and **"resolve remaining open issues during the iteration."** That remedy *is* the human asking-questions-and-adapting behavior — the exact capability the asymmetry says agents lack.
- **Scrum Alliance, "Pros and Cons of a Definition of Ready"** — https://resources.scrumalliance.org/Article/pros-cons-definition-ready. A rigid DoR "acts like a gate, blocking certain backlog items… until all of the pre-work… is completed," producing waterfall-like delay. Again: about humans, opinion-grade.
- **Contrary signal even within human agile — Jeff Sutherland** ("Ready: The Dynamic Model of Scrum," http://jeffsutherland.com/scrum/2009/07/ready-dynamic-model-of-scrum.html): the Scrum co-creator argues a *strong* Ready state prevents team thrashing and (per the Scrum Papers) roughly doubles velocity. So even for humans the anti-pattern claim is contested, not settled.

**The agent-side evidence shows agents default to confidently fabricating missing detail rather than asking — the asymmetry is real and empirical.**

- **"Learning to Ask: When LLM Agents Meet Unclear Instruction,"** Wang et al., EMNLP 2025 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.00557. Key finding: "due to the next-token prediction training objective, LLMs tend to **arbitrarily generate the missed argument, which may lead to hallucinations and risks**." This is the mechanism: the agent invents the under-specified piece instead of pausing.
- **QuestBench,** Kim et al. (MIT/DeepMind), 2025 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.22674. Models that solve fully-specified problems are weak at knowing *what to ask*: only **40–50% accuracy on Logic-Q and Planning-Q**, and the paper states "the ability to solve well-specified reasoning problems may not be sufficient… models have difficulty identifying the right question to ask, even when they can solve the fully specified version." Agents are weakest precisely at the clarification a human does reflexively.
- **"What Prompts Don't Say: Understanding and Managing Underspecification,"** Yang et al. (CMU), 2025 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13360. Relying on the agent to infer the unsaid is unstable: under-specified prompts are "2x as likely to regress across model or prompt changes," with accuracy drops "exceeding 20%." So "the agent will just adapt like a human" is empirically fragile.
- **"Ask or Assume?"** Edwards & Schuster, 2026 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.26233. States the asymmetry outright: "human developers naturally resolve underspecification by asking clarifying questions, while current agents are **largely optimized for autonomous execution**." An uncertainty-aware multi-agent scaffold recovers most of the lost ground (69.4% resolve rate vs. a single-agent baseline on underspecified SWE-bench), i.e., the gap is real *and* addressable by adding a gating/clarification stage.
- **Practitioner convergence (opinion, but aligned with the empirics):** the spec-driven-development movement (Augment Code, Addy Osmani/O'Reilly, Microsoft Spec Kit) and CodeRabbit's "hidden cost of AI coding agents" (https://www.coderabbit.ai/blog/the-hidden-cost-of-ai-coding-agents-isnt-from-ai-at-all) argue agents need *more* upfront constraint than humans because "they don't stop to check whether requirements were vague… they just proceed confidently," and "catching the flaw before execution is consistently cheaper than unwinding a confidently wrong implementation."

**Design implication:** The anti-pattern argument is human-specific and rests on a capability (in-flight adaptation / asking) that agents demonstrably lack and are *trained against*. A readiness/plan gate for agents is not the stage-gate anti-pattern Cohn warns about — it substitutes for a missing human reflex. **Verdict on Thread 1: does not transfer; a plan gate is justified for agents even though discouraged for humans.** (Caveat: human-side material is all practitioner opinion; the agent-side empirical work is recent and partly 2025–2026 preprints.)

---

## THREAD 2 — Error compounding: why a *plan-time* gate is the highest-leverage place to catch a defect

**The geometric floor (independent steps):** end-to-end success = p^N (Lusser's Law / series reliability). The canonical worked numbers: at **95% per step, 10 steps → ~60%, 20 steps → ~36%**; at 90%/step, 5 steps ≈ 59% ("a coin flip"). These appear consistently across practitioner explainers (e.g., MindStudio, https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/multi-agent-reliability-compounding-problem-77-percent) but the formula itself is standard reliability theory.

**The peer-reviewed law (strongest source):** "The Illusion of Diminishing Returns: Measuring Long Horizon Execution in LLMs," Sinha et al., ICLR 2026 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.09677. Verified verbatim: "even marginal gains in single-step accuracy can compound into **exponential improvements in the length of tasks** a model can successfully complete." Formally H_s(p) = ln(s)/ln(p). Critically, it shows real decay is *worse* than the independent model: "the per-step accuracy of models degrades as the number of steps increases. This is not just due to long-context limitations — curiously, we observe a **self-conditioning effect — models become more likely to make mistakes when the context contains their errors from prior turns.**" An early error doesn't just cost one step; it raises the probability of *future* errors.

**The empirical curve and decay model:**
- **METR, "Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks,"** Kwa et al., 2025 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14499 / https://metr.org/blog/2025-03-19-measuring-ai-ability-to-complete-long-tasks/. Defines a model's "50% time horizon" (task length at which success = 50%); near-100% success on <4-minute tasks collapses to <10% on tasks >~4 hours. Horizon has been doubling ~every 7 months.
- **"Is there a half-life for the success rates of AI agents?"** Toby Ord, 2025 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05115. Models a constant per-step hazard rate → success = (1/2)^(t/half-life), fitting the METR data. The mechanism: longer tasks contain "increasingly large sets of subtasks where failing any one fails the task."

**Cascades and the plan-time vs. execution-time trade-off:**
- **"Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" (MAST),** Cemri et al. (UC Berkeley), 2025 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657. 14 failure modes in 3 categories (Specification, Inter-Agent Misalignment, Task Verification) from 150+ traces, inter-annotator κ=0.88. Notes failures "may have a cascading effect." **Caveat to flag:** the widely-quoted "42%/37%/21%" category split circulating in secondary blogs is **not** a clean verified primary figure — cite MAST for the 14-modes/3-category taxonomy and κ=0.88, not that split.
- **"When Should Users Check?"** Zhou et al., 2026 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.05307. A decision-theoretic model of confirmation frequency that formalizes catching errors earlier to reduce downstream propagation cost — the literal plan-time-vs-runtime verification trade-off.
- Mechanistic backing that one early error contaminates the whole chain: stepwise reasoning error-propagation work (e.g., https://arxiv.org/html/2412.11934v3).

**Design implication:** A plan is the root of the dependency tree; a flawed plan doesn't fail one step, it sets a low p that the whole N-step trajectory is multiplied against — and self-conditioning makes the realized decay worse than p^N. Catching a defect at plan time (one cheap critic call) prevents N steps of compounding *and* the error-amplification that follows the first mistake. This is the strongest economic argument for the gate.

---

## THREAD 3 — Separate critic vs. self-critique: the central question. Separate wins.

**(a) Self-preference / self-enhancement bias is real and measured — a model judging its own output is biased.**
- **"Judging LLM-as-a-Judge,"** Zheng et al., NeurIPS 2023 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685. Verified verbatim from the body: "**GPT-4 favors itself with a 10% higher win rate; Claude-v1 favors itself with a 25% higher win rate**," and "**GPT-3.5 does not favor itself.**" **Important honesty caveat (also verified verbatim):** "Due to limited data and small differences, our study cannot determine whether the models exhibit a self-enhancement bias." So this is suggestive, not conclusive — do not overstate it.
- The effect is corroborated by stronger later work: **"LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations,"** Panickssery et al., NeurIPS 2024 (oral) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.13076 — finds a "linear correlation between self-recognition capability and the strength of self-preference bias"; and **"Self-Preference Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge,"** Wataoka et al., 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.21819 — traces the bias to low perplexity / familiarity (models prefer text in their own style).

**(b) Intrinsic self-correction (no external feedback) is flat-to-negative.**
- **"LLMs Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet,"** Huang et al. (DeepMind), ICLR 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01798. Verified verbatim: "LLMs struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback, and at times, **their performance even degrades after self-correction.**" Their definition of intrinsic self-correction is correction "based solely on its inherent capabilities, **without the crutch of external feedback**." The paper's central diagnosis is that prior "successful" self-correction smuggled in an **oracle label** (ground truth used to decide when to stop) — remove the oracle and the gains vanish or reverse. The model cannot reliably judge its own correctness.

**(c) Self-correction WITHOUT external grounding is the failure case; tools/grounding fix it.**
- **CRITIC,** Gou et al., ICLR 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.11738. Bottom line: "our research **highlights the crucial importance of external feedback** in promoting the ongoing self-improvement of LLMs." Self-correction works when grounded in external tools (search for facts, code interpreter for debugging), not introspection.
- Survey corroboration — **"When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes?"** Kamoi et al., TACL 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.01297: "no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs" (except tasks exceptionally suited to it), while "self-correction works well in tasks that can use **reliable external feedback**." "The bottleneck is in the feedback generation."

**(d) Reflexion and Self-Refine — the discriminator: one secretly uses an external signal, the other is the cautionary tale.**
- **Self-Refine,** Madaan et al., NeurIPS 2023 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17651 — is the *genuine* intrinsic method: "a single LLM as the generator, refiner, and feedback provider," no external signal by design. Its documented Achilles' heel is exactly self-bias, no reliable stopping signal, and degradation on hard reasoning without external feedback.
- **Reflexion,** Shinn et al., NeurIPS 2023 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11366 — looks self-improving but its reflection is computed *on an external signal*: unit-test pass/fail (HumanEval, 91% pass@1), environment success (ALFWorld, +22%), reward. The abstract names "**external or internally simulated**" feedback sources explicitly. So Reflexion's flagship wins are not pure self-feedback — they ride on an external verifier/test. **Design takeaway: the methods that "work" are the ones with an external signal; the one that's purely self-referential (Self-Refine) is where self-bias bites.**

**(e) LLM-Modulo — the affirmative thesis: generators good, self-verifiers unreliable, use a sound external verifier.**
- **"LLMs Can't Plan, But Can Help Planning in LLM-Modulo Frameworks,"** Kambhampati et al., ICML 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01817. Core thesis: "auto-regressive LLMs **cannot, by themselves, do planning or self-verification**," but they generate good candidate solutions "albeit with no guarantees." The architecture pairs the LLM generator with **external sound model-based verifiers** in a Generate-Test-Critique back-prompting loop; "the soundness of the LLM-modulo framework is **inherited from the soundness of the critics**."
- The hard empirical backing — **"On the Self-Verification Limitations of LLMs,"** Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati, 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.08115. Verified verbatim: "**significant performance collapse with self-critique and significant performance gains with sound external verification**," across Game of 24, Graph Coloring, STRIPS planning (GPT-4); "merely re-prompting with a **sound verifier** maintains most of the benefits." This directly answers the central question: self-critique made it *worse*; an external verifier made it better.

**Design implication for Thread 3:** Do not let the executing agent grade its own plan. Self-preference bias (a), the inability to judge one's own correctness (b), and the self-critique performance *collapse* (e) all point the same way. The critic must be a **separate role**, and it is strongest when it can invoke **external grounding** (tests, schema/constraint checks, tool-verified facts, or a sound checker) rather than pure LLM introspection. A bare "second LLM, no tools" critic still helps by breaking self-preference and self-recognition, but the largest, most reliable gains come from giving the critic external verification capability.

---

## THREAD 4 — Plan verification before execution is an established distinct phase

- **Plan-and-Solve prompting,** Wang et al., ACL 2023 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.04091. Splits "devising a plan to divide the entire task into smaller subtasks" from "carrying out the subtasks," explicitly targeting **missing-step errors**; beats Zero-shot-CoT by a large margin. The foundational "plan first" result.
- **Plan-and-Execute agents (LangGraph)** — https://www.langchain.com/blog/planning-agents. A distinct planner + executor + **replanner**; claimed benefits include quality from "forcing the planner to explicitly 'think through' all the steps." Establishes the full plan as a reviewable artifact before any action.
- **ReWOO,** Xu et al., 2023 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18323. Generates the *entire* plan before any tool call; **5× token efficiency and +4% accuracy on HotpotQA**. Evidence that committing to a complete, inspectable plan up front is both cheaper and (modestly) more accurate — the plan is exactly the right artifact to gate on.
- **"Understanding the planning of LLM agents: A survey,"** Huang et al., 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.02716. Taxonomizes agent planning into Task Decomposition, Plan Selection, **External Module** (model-based verifiers external to the LLM), **Reflection**, and Memory — i.e., the field already treats external verification and reflection on plans as categories distinct from plan generation.
- **TravelPlanner,** Xie/Zhang et al., ICML 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01622. Verified verbatim: "**even GPT-4 only achieves a success rate of 0.6%**" (1,225 intents, ~4M records). Failures are dominated by inability to "keep track of multiple constraints." The brutal headline number for why naive agent planning fails.
- **LLM-Modulo on TravelPlanning,** Gundawar et al., 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.20625. Verified verbatim: "Chain of Thought, ReAct, and Reflexion achieve a meager **0%, 0.6%, and 0%** with GPT3.5-Turbo," while the external-critic LLM-Modulo setup gives "**4.6x for GPT4-Turbo**" and lifts GPT-3.5-Turbo "**from 0% to 5%**." Note Reflexion (self-reflection) scoring **0%** here while the external-verifier architecture wins — a clean head-to-head for separate-critic over self-critique on planning.
- **The strongest plan-critic number — "Can LLMs Really Improve by Self-critiquing Their Own Plans?"** Valmeekam, Marquez, Kambhampati, 2023 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.08118. Abstract (verified): "**self-critiquing appears to diminish plan generation performance, especially when compared to systems with external, sound verifiers**," and the LLM verifiers "produce a notable number of false positives." The body numbers (Blocksworld): LLM plan-verifier ~61% binary accuracy, **38 false positives out of 45 invalid plans** (it approves invalid plans ~84% of the time), and end-to-end **LLM self-critique 55% vs. LLM + sound external verifier (VAL) 88%** — a 33-point gap. This is the single most direct piece of evidence for the gate: an LLM grading its own plan routinely waves invalid plans through.
- Plan-verification as a named pre-execution phase also appears explicitly in robotics — **VerifyLLM** (https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.05118) verifies a pre-generated action sequence *before* execution using temporal logic — and in **PlanBench** (https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.10498), which treats plan verification as a first-class task mechanically checkable via VAL.

**Design implication:** The plan is a concrete, inspectable artifact (you already store it in the ticket), and the literature treats verifying it as a distinct phase. The decisive caution: the verifier's **false-positive rate** is the metric that matters — a critic that approves bad plans is worse than none, because it manufactures false confidence. Where any part of the plan is mechanically checkable (file paths exist, referenced symbols resolve, acceptance criteria present, dependency/constraint satisfaction), route it to a *sound* check rather than to LLM judgment.

---

## Synthesized verdict

**Does the evidence support a SEPARATE-critic, plan-time gate for autonomous agents?** Yes, robustly, on four independent legs:

1. **It does not contradict the agile anti-pattern.** That critique is human-specific opinion whose safety depends on in-flight human adaptation — a capability agents empirically lack and are trained against (Wang 2409.00557, QuestBench 2503.22674, Yang 2505.13360). For agents, the gate replaces a missing reflex.
2. **The economics favor plan time.** Errors compound geometrically and worse (Sinha 2509.09677's self-conditioning; METR 2503.14499; Ord 2505.05115). A defect in the plan multiplies through the whole N-step trajectory; catching it with one critic call is the highest-leverage intervention.
3. **Separate beats self.** Self-preference bias (Zheng 2306.05685), inability to judge own correctness (Huang 2310.01798), self-critique *collapse* (Stechly 2402.08115), and LLM plan-verifiers approving 84% of invalid plans (Valmeekam 2310.08118) all say: the executor must not grade its own plan, and the critic is strongest with external grounding (CRITIC 2305.11738; LLM-Modulo 2402.01817).
4. **It's a recognized distinct phase** with demonstrated value (Plan-and-Solve, ReWOO's 5×/+4%, the survey's taxonomy, and the LLM-Modulo TravelPlanning sweep where the external-critic architecture beats self-reflection 0%→5%).

**Should it BLOCK or ADVISE?** A graduated stance the evidence supports:

- **BLOCK on sound, mechanical checks.** Where a plan defect is *deterministically* detectable (missing acceptance criteria, non-existent file paths, unresolved symbols, violated hard dependencies/constraints), the gate should be hard-blocking — these are "sound verifiers" in Kambhampati's sense, with near-zero false positives, and they are exactly the class of error agents cascade on.
- **ADVISE (soft / route-to-clarification) on LLM-judgment findings.** Where the critic is an LLM reasoning about plan quality, its **false-positive AND false-negative rates are non-trivial** (Valmeekam 61%; Zheng's own caveat that self-enhancement isn't even conclusively established). A hard block here re-imports the very stage-gate thrash the agile critique warns about — now driven by an *unreliable* gatekeeper. Better: surface findings as blocking-by-default-but-overridable, or convert low-confidence findings into clarifying questions back to the originating context (the agent analogue of the human "ask and adapt" that the whole asymmetry is built on).

In short: **separate critic, yes; plan-time, yes; block on what a sound verifier can prove, advise on what only an LLM can opine.** The single biggest implementation risk the literature flags is a critic that confidently approves bad plans (false positives) — so the gate's own verifier should be evaluated and tuned on its false-positive rate before it is trusted to block.

**Evidence caveats:** the human-agile side is all practitioner opinion; the Zheng self-enhancement figures carry the authors' explicit "cannot determine conclusively" caveat; the MAST "42/37/21" split is unverified secondary material (the 14-mode/3-category taxonomy and κ=0.88 are solid); and several supporting agent papers are 2025–2026 preprints not yet peer-reviewed. The core load-bearing claims (2310.01798, 2402.08115, 2310.08118, 2402.01622, 2405.20625, 2509.09677, 2306.05685) were each verified verbatim against the primary source.

=== RESEARCH REPORT ===
=== GitHub: agentic plan/execute split survey (Aider/Cline/OpenHands/etc.)
=== agent aaa8566d7c4f36417

All six research streams returned with strong primary-source grounding. I have comprehensive coverage. Let me synthesize the findings into the requested report.

---

# Plan-Verification Patterns in Coding Agents: Research Findings

A survey of how popular, actively-maintained coding-agent projects handle the planning→execution boundary, plan review/critique, and plan-approval gates — with a focus on your three special interests: (1) a **separate critic/reviewer agent** reviewing a plan before execution, (2) plans that must **name files/tests/dependencies** before acting, and (3) **probes/spikes/experiments at plan time**.

The headline finding up front, because it reframes your design space: **almost nobody ships an automated separate-agent plan-critic gate.** Across 18 projects, the planner/executor split is overwhelmingly *one agent loop with a swapped system prompt + restricted toolset*, and the enforced gate is *human approval*, not a reviewing model. Automated plan-critique exists only as wire-it-yourself framework patterns (LangGraph reflection/reflexion, AutoGen critic). The closest things to your "separate reviewer agent reviews the plan" idea are post-hoc evaluators (OpenHands critic, SWE-agent reviewer) that score *completed work*, not pre-execution plans. This is a genuine gap — which means rebar's plan-verification step would be a relatively novel mechanism, not a me-too feature. Build it deliberately.

---

## Per-project findings

Legend for the four questions: **(a)** planning a distinct phase? **(b)** planner a separate agent/model? **(c)** plan-review/critique or human-approval gate? **(d)** probes/experiments at plan time?

### Turnkey coding agents

**Aider** — https://github.com/Aider-AI/aider · ~46.4k★ · maintained but coasting (latest release v0.86.0 Aug 2025; recent commits are model-list housekeeping)
- (a) Conceptual only — architect+editor are two sequential model calls in one automated turn, not a user-facing phase.
- (b) **Yes, two separate models.** The *architect model* describes the solution in natural language; the *editor model* (`--editor-model`) translates that into structured file edits. This is the canonical generator/executor split you cited.
- (c) **No gate.** The architect's proposal flows straight into the editor — no human checkpoint, no reviewing model between them. Critical read: this split is about *competence* (pair a reasoning-strong model with an edit-reliable one), **not governance**. (Aider's general git auto-commit/shell-confirm safety nets are not architect-specific.)
- (d) No. The architect emits prose from existing context (repo map + added files); no exploration loop.

**Claude Code** — plan mode / ExitPlanMode · Anthropic, actively developed (docs reference v2.1.x, mid-2026)
- (a) **Yes, a first-class enforced permission-mode state** you enter (`Shift+Tab` / `/plan` / `--permission-mode plan`) and exit by approving.
- (b) **Same model, restricted to read-only** — not a separate planner agent. Write tools are withheld until approval. (The read-only guarantee is policy/prompt-enforced, not a hard sandbox.)
- (c) **Human-approved**, not agent-reviewed. ExitPlanMode surfaces approve/refine options; `Ctrl+G` lets you edit the plan yourself. The auto-mode action classifier is a *different* feature (reviews individual actions at exec time, not the plan). The one model-mediated path — Ultraplan browser review — is still human-gated.
- (d) **Read-only but not inert** — Claude *can run exploratory shell commands and read files* while planning; it just can't edit source. Notable nuance vs. Aider: "read-only" ≠ "no execution."

**OpenHands** (formerly OpenDevin) — https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands · ~77.7k★ · very active (release 1.8.0, Jun 2026). **Critical structural note: the agent logic moved to a separate SDK repo** (software-agent-sdk, ~827★); write-ups describing `agenthub/` classes describe the dead V0 monolith.
- (a) No — interleaved ReAct, no enforced plan-then-execute boundary. Planning survives only as discretionary in-loop tools (a TodoWrite-style `TaskTrackerTool`, an opt-in `PlanningFileEditorTool`); nothing gates on them.
- (b) No. CodeActAgent is the single ReAct executor. **The old `PlannerAgent` was removed (PR #5959, Jan 2025)** — a planner agent was tried and *deleted*. Delegation exists but is off by default and homogeneous (sub-agent-as-tool).
- (c) No plan-level gate. There's per-*action* confirmation (mid-loop, per-command) and a `critic/` that scores *completed* work for retry — a **post-hoc evaluator, not a pre-execution plan critic.**
- (d) No distinct de-risking stage; exploration is ordinary in-loop ReAct.

**SWE-agent** (Princeton) — https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent · ~19.6k★ · maintenance mode (v1.1.0 May 2025; team's active focus is mini-SWE-agent)
- (a) No — explicitly ReAct (thought+action interleaved), cited by name in the paper.
- (b) No — single agent, single model. `RetryAgent` is best-of-N of the same config, not planner+executor.
- (c) None at plan time. The `reviewer.py` machinery is **post-hoc best-of-N submission selection** (score finished trajectories 1–5), easy to mistake for plan critique but isn't one.
- (d) Emergent, not designed — trajectories happen to start with reproduce/localize, but it's interleaved, not an instrumented phase. The real engineering is the **ACI** (windowed viewer, search caps, edit-with-linter), not planning.
- *Contrast worth keeping:* **Agentless** (deliberately non-agentic fixed localize→repair→validate pipeline) and **AutoCodeRover** (bounded agency: a dedicated AST-aware retrieval phase separated from a patch phase) sit at the low-agency end of the spectrum.

**Cline** — https://github.com/cline/cline · ~63.5k★ · very actively maintained (multiple releases Jun 2026)
- (a) **Yes — explicit Plan ↔ Act toggle.** Plan explores/strategizes; Act executes. History carries across the switch.
- (b) **Different model per mode is first-class and configurable** ("Use different models for Plan and Act" — e.g. a strong reasoner to plan, a fast model to execute; auto-swaps on toggle). It's the same agent loop with swapped model + prompt. **Plan mode is genuinely no-edit/no-exec** (real tool gating).
- (c) Two gates: a *soft* mode-boundary (human flips the toggle when "aligned" — no enforced approval artifact) and the *hard, substantive* one — **per-action approval** of every edit/command during Act (relaxable via auto-approve).
- (d) **Yes — and the strongest named flow in the set:** `/deep-planning` runs (1) silent codebase investigation → (2) clarifying-question discussion → (3) generate an `implementation_plan.md` artifact → (4) spin up a tracked task. Exploration-grounded, produces a written plan.

**Roo Code** — https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code · ~24.2k★ · **DISCONTINUED — repo archived May 15, 2026** (points users back to Cline; live descendant is Kilo Code)
- (a) Yes — multiple persona modes (Architect=plan, Code=execute, plus Ask/Debug/Orchestrator).
- (b) Per-mode *remembered* model (not a single dual-model toggle). **Finer-grained tool gating than Cline:** Architect mode = read + mcp + `edit` *regex-restricted to markdown only*. The **Orchestrator/Boomerang** mode delegates via `new_task` to isolated per-mode subtasks; results return via `attempt_completion`. (Delegation is per-mode, not per-model.)
- (c) No plan-approval gate; per-action approval during execution is the real gate.
- (d) Architect reads code while planning; no named deep-planning protocol like Cline's.

**Continue** — https://github.com/continuedev/continue · ~34.1k★ · very actively maintained (commits Jun 2026). **Most source-verifiable of the open agents.**
- (a) **Yes — a read-only-restricted Plan mode** (`"chat" | "agent" | "plan" | "background"`). The toolset is literally filtered to read-only built-in tools in source (`selectActiveTools.ts`). ⚠️ Caveat: the filter only covers built-in tools — **MCP tools pass through unfiltered**, relying on the prompt alone. (A real lesson for your design: tool-level enforcement beats prompt-level, and gaps matter.)
- (b) No — same loop, mode swaps toolset + system message.
- (c) Per-tool policies: **Ask First (default) / Automatic / Excluded**; edits and bash default to "ask."
- (d) Yes — read/grep/glob/semantic-search stay active in Plan mode.

**Cursor** (agent mode) — closed; cursor.com/docs · proprietary, no source/stars
- (a) **Yes — Plan Mode** (recent, ~v2.2): produces a **reviewable, editable Markdown plan** saved to `.cursor/plans/` with structured to-dos.
- (b) No — same Agent, different mode.
- (c) **Plan-approval gate** ("Click to build" — execution starts only on that click), plus a command gate. ⚠️ Default Run Mode is **Auto-review** (auto-runs allowlisted commands, file edits auto-apply); strict per-command approval requires opting into Allowlist mode. The marketing implies more friction than defaults deliver.
- (d) Yes — researches the codebase, asks clarifying questions before emitting the plan.

**Devin / Cognition** — closed; docs.devin.ai · proprietary, claims are doc/blog-sourced (not auditable)
- (a) **Yes — "Interactive Planning"** (named feature: build detailed plans before coding).
- (b) Not disclosed (described as a single agent with a planning *phase*).
- (c) **Soft/configurable approval** — "wait for my approval" button gated by an Agency setting, with a **30-second auto-proceed timeout** by default. The confidence-score (🟢🟡🔴) gating claim is **blog-only marketing**, absent from core docs.
- (d) Yes — "Initial Assessment" indexes the branch and searches for relevant files before proposing.

**GPT-Engineer** — https://github.com/gpt-engineer-org/gpt-engineer · ~55.2k★ but **ARCHIVED / EOL** (succeeded by lovable.dev; last push May 2025)
- (a) No — linear prompt-chaining; "planning" is a prompt directive inside one generation call.
- (b) No — single agent.
- (c) Opt-in `--clarify` Q&A loop before generating; always-on execute/apply-diff gates. No review of the generated source itself.
- (d) No — default generates a fresh project with zero exploration.

**GPT Pilot (Pythagora)** — https://github.com/Pythagora-io/gpt-pilot · ~33.7k★ but **STAGNANT** ("not being maintained anymore") and ⚠️ **had a supply-chain compromise** (malicious telemetry payload ~Aug 2025, patched Jun 2026 — rotate credentials if run from source in that window). Despite the health caveats, **architecturally the richest multi-role pipeline in the set** — worth studying as a design reference.
- (a) **Yes, multi-stage**, enforced by an **Orchestrator state machine** (not the agents): Wizard → SpecWriter → Architect → TechLead (breaks epic into a `DevelopmentPlan` of `Task`s) → Developer (decomposes a task into concrete steps) → CodeMonkey/Executor → Troubleshooter/BugHunter.
- (b) **Yes — genuinely separate planner roles** (Architect + TechLead produce the plan; Developer decomposes each task into a structured `TaskSteps` list). ⚠️ The README's "Reviewer"/"Product Owner"/"Debugger" agents have no source files — they map onto other agents.
- (c) **Many hard human gates** (the strongest of the set): approve spec → confirm architecture/deps → **review task breakdown** ("Are you happy with the breakdown?") → approve/edit/skip each task → per-step intervention → an LLM code-review inside CodeMonkey → test the running app.
- (d) **Yes — and the only one that probes the *environment*, not just the repo:** SpecWriter clarifies, a relevant-files mixin identifies files before coding, and **the Architect actually runs each dependency's `test` command to probe the host environment.** This is the closest thing in the survey to a plan-time spike.

### Frameworks (planning/critique primitives)

**LangGraph** — https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph · ~35.2k★ · active (Jun 2026)
- (a)/(b) Plan-and-execute (`planner → agent → replan` graph, separate node/model/schema) is a **tutorial pattern, not a built-in**.
- (c) **Reflection / Reflexion (separate generator + critic loop) are tutorial recipes, not shipped classes** — Reflexion (arXiv 2303.11366) is notable: a structured `Reflection` schema with `missing`/`superfluous` fields, grounded by external search between draft and revise. The *shipped* primitive is human-in-the-loop: `interrupt()` + `Command(resume=...)` (approve/reject/edit state) — the enforced gate is whatever you build on it.
- (d) None — the planner is a single static structured-output call.

**AutoGen** — https://github.com/microsoft/autogen · ~59.1k★ · ⚠️ ~2 months stale (last push Apr 2026; converging into the Microsoft Agent Framework)
- (a)/(b) **The one genuinely shipped planner: Magentic-One's Orchestrator** — an outer planning loop builds a **Task Ledger** (facts + plan) before an inner execution loop runs against a **Progress Ledger**; re-plans on stall via `max_stalls`. Orchestrator plans/tracks and never executes; WebSurfer/FileSurfer/Coder execute.
- (c) **No canonical built-in Critic class** — assistant+critic reflection is always two ordinary agents (composable via `register_nested_chats` / `SocietyOfMindAgent`). The only built-in gate is human approval (`UserProxyAgent` / `human_input_mode` / `approval_func`). Magentic-One re-plans on stalls but never submits its plan to a separate critic before executing.
- (d) **Yes — the best plan-time epistemics in the set:** the Task Ledger prompt explicitly separates `GIVEN/VERIFIED FACTS` vs `FACTS TO LOOK UP` vs `FACTS TO DERIVE` vs `EDUCATED GUESSES` *before committing the plan*. It's a to-do list of probes, not speculative execution — but it's a structured way to force a plan to declare its unknowns.

**CrewAI** — https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI · ~53.9k★ · active (Jun 2026)
- (a)/(b) **Shipped, real:** `Crew(planning=True)` runs a dedicated planner `Agent` ("Task Execution Planner") with its own `planning_llm` once before any task, producing a typed `PlanPerTask` per task — but it's then **string-concatenated onto each task's description** (becomes prompt text, no separate plan object).
- (c) **No gate over the plan itself.** Review mechanisms gate *outputs*: a hierarchical manager agent reviews worker output; **task guardrails** are a genuine validate→reject→retry loop (`guardrail_max_retries`); `human_input=True` gates the final answer. No dedicated critic primitive.
- (d) None — the planner has no tools; it's one static call over a stringified task summary.

**MetaGPT** — https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT · ~68.9k★ · maintenance/low-activity (pivoted commercially to atoms.dev; core pipeline work stopped ~mid-2025)
- (a) Real artifact pipeline (PRD → design → tasks → code) but **no explicit phase boundary in code** — ordering emerges from message subscriptions, no controller/gate.
- (b) Separate `Role` instances with distinct prompts, but **typically the same underlying LLM** (model-separation is supported, not default). The "assembly line" is a shared message pool, not direct calls.
- (c) ⚠️ **The most over-marketed review story in the survey.** Review *action classes exist but are dead/unwired code*: `DesignReview`, `WritePRDReview`, `WriteReview` (which even has an explicit `LGTM`/`LBTM` verdict) are imported only by tests — **no role ever calls them.** The only review that runs is post-plan, code-level `WriteCodeReview` — opt-in, advisory, and it never blocks (returns code regardless of verdict after k iterations). There is no Architect-reviews-PRD gate.
- (d) No — planning roles only call the LLM to emit text; executable feedback is QA-stage only.

**Plandex** — https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex · ~15.5k★ · ⚠️ low-activity/wind-down (main dormant ~8 months; Plandex Cloud wound down Oct 2025)
- (a) Partial — plans are first-class objects with a **sandbox of pending diffs**, but the tentative state is the *file write to disk*, not a pre-approved plan (the model has already planned and coded).
- (b) **Yes — genuine model-level role separation:** 9 roles incl. distinct `planner` vs `coder` vs `architect` vs `builder`. ⚠️ But "Opus plans, Sonnet codes" is a *non-default* pack; the shipped default shares Sonnet across planner/coder and downshifts only mechanical roles to cheap models. **No `verifier` role exists.**
- (c) **Human diff-review** before apply (`diff` → `apply`/`reject`); no automated semantic gate; **bypassed entirely at full autonomy.**
- (d) Real but post-apply: `debug` repeatedly runs a command and fixes until it passes — an *apply→run→debug* self-heal loop **after** changes land, not a probe that informs the plan.

---

## Ranked: the most reusable, battle-tested patterns for a separate-agent plan-review gate

Ranked by how proven *and* how directly reusable for your specific goal (a reviewer agent critiquing a plan before execution). I've been honest about which are "proven in production" vs. "proven as a pattern."

**1. Read-only planner with hard tool-gating, not prompt-gating — proven by Continue (and Cline).**
The dominant production design isn't a separate agent; it's *one model in a mode where write/exec tools are physically removed from the toolset*. Continue implements this as a literal tool filter in source; Cline makes Plan mode no-edit/no-exec. The reusable lesson for rebar: **enforce your reviewer's read-only/no-side-effect constraint at the tool layer, not in the prompt** — and mind Continue's documented gap (MCP tools slipped past the built-in filter). If your reviewer agent runs probes, gate exactly what it can touch. This is the single most battle-tested primitive here.

**2. Separate planner role that emits a structured, decomposed plan artifact — proven by GPT Pilot (Architect/TechLead → `DevelopmentPlan`/`Task`s) and CrewAI (`planning=True` → typed `PlanPerTask`).**
If you want a plan that *names files/tests/dependencies before acting* (your interest #2), the proven move is a dedicated planner role that outputs a **typed/structured plan object** (not free prose), which a downstream step — your reviewer — can mechanically check field-by-field. GPT Pilot's TechLead-decomposes-epic-into-tasks and CrewAI's Pydantic `PlanPerTask` are the two shipped exemplars. rebar already has the substrate for this (acceptance-criteria blocks, `set_file_impact`, `set_verify_commands`) — a structured plan that *must* populate those is directly in line with this pattern, and would make a reviewer's job checkable rather than vibes-based.

**3. Generator + separate critic loop with a structured critique schema — proven as a pattern by LangGraph Reflexion and AutoGen reflection (and as the discriminating case AGAINST MetaGPT).**
This is the closest match to your core goal, and the honest finding is **no turnkey coding agent ships it — it exists only as framework patterns.** The reusable design: a *separate* critic model, prompted as an adversarial reviewer, emits a **structured verdict** (LangGraph Reflexion's `missing`/`superfluous` fields; a `LGTM`/`LBTM`-style verdict) that the planner must address before the plan is accepted. MetaGPT is the cautionary tale: it *wrote* exactly these classes (`WriteReview` with LGTM/LBTM) and **never wired them in** — so the lesson is that a critic only counts if it's on the enforced path and its verdict actually blocks. Your rebar context already has the better building blocks here: the **completion-verifier agent** (PASS/FAIL with per-finding source citations) is precisely a structured-critique-with-verdict mechanism — applying that same shape to *plans* (not just completions) is the natural, defensible extension, and would put rebar ahead of every project surveyed.

**4. Pre-plan epistemic ledger that forces the plan to declare unknowns — proven by AutoGen Magentic-One's Task Ledger.**
Before committing a plan, force it to enumerate `VERIFIED FACTS` vs `FACTS TO LOOK UP` vs `FACTS TO DERIVE` vs `EDUCATED GUESSES`. This is the most reusable *de-risking* pattern (your interest #3 without needing to execute code): a reviewer agent can specifically attack the "educated guesses" and "facts to look up" — the exact places a plan is most likely wrong. Cheap, model-only, no sandbox required, and it makes plan risk legible to a critic.

**5. Plan-time environment probe (a real spike), not just a repo read — proven (narrowly) by GPT Pilot's Architect running dependency `test` commands; supported by Claude Code/Cline/Cursor read-and-explore planning.**
True plan-time *experiments* are rare. GPT Pilot's Architect actually executing each dependency's test command to probe the host is the only genuine environment-spike in the survey. Most others (Claude Code, Cline `/deep-planning`, Cursor, Devin) probe by *reading/searching* the codebase, which de-risks file/symbol assumptions but not runtime ones. If you want rebar's planner/reviewer to run a real spike, GPT Pilot is your precedent — and pattern #1 (hard tool-gating) is the prerequisite that makes letting a planner execute *safe*.

### The strategic takeaway for your design
Your instinct is sound and the space is open: **a separate reviewer agent that critiques a plan before execution is, today, essentially unbuilt in shipping coding agents** — the field stops at human-approval gates (Claude Code, Cline, Cursor, Devin, GPT Pilot) and post-hoc work-scoring critics (OpenHands, SWE-agent). The reusable ingredients all exist but are scattered: read-only tool-gating (Continue/Cline), structured plan artifacts (GPT Pilot/CrewAI), structured critique verdicts (LangGraph Reflexion / rebar's own completion-verifier), and epistemic ledgers (Magentic-One). rebar is unusually well-positioned to combine them because it already has the structured-ticket substrate (`set_file_impact`, `set_verify_commands`, AC blocks) and a HMAC-signed PASS/FAIL verifier agent — turning that verifier on *plans* rather than only *completions* is the highest-leverage, most-defensible version of what you're proposing.

A repeated caveat to carry forward: **distinguish shipped-and-enforced from written-but-dead and tutorial-only.** MetaGPT's reviewers are dead code; LangGraph/AutoGen critics are patterns you assemble; CrewAI/AutoGen-Magentic-One/GPT-Pilot planners are the only genuinely shipped separate planners. Design rebar's gate so the verdict is *on the enforced path and actually blocks* — that's the line MetaGPT crossed on paper but not in code.
